title: The Milky Way seen from the Atacama Desert
caption: The Milky Way at twilight over the Atacama Desert, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at ALMA, Chajnantor plateau, Chile

recognition.text: Published in the ESO image archive. No published rating.

story: The Milky Way emerges at twilight over the Atacama Desert. Directly over the rock in the middle of the frame sits the Large Magellanic Cloud, a neighbouring galaxy of the Milky Way, and above it lies the reddish spot of the bright Carina Nebula, a glowing cloud of gas.

Further left, along the plane of the Milky Way, you can spot the Southern Cross with the Coal Sack. The Coal Sack is a dark cloud of dust that blocks the starlight behind it. Next come two bright stars, Beta and Alpha Centauri.
The Atacama Desert has hosted ESO's observatories since the 1960s, and it is the chosen site for the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT), which ESO calls the world's biggest eye on the sky.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based twilight photograph by G. Hüdepohl. The source does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: In twilight the eye picks out only brighter objects, while a camera gathering light over time may also record the Carina Nebula's reddish colour.

alt: The Milky Way in a twilight sky above a desert rock, with a fuzzy patch just above the rock, a reddish spot above that and two bright stars to the left.
